scenario: AITA got refusing to back up for someone who drove the wrong way up to an ATM? | My bank has kind of an odd set up for their ATM out front. It’s in a small cut out with clearly marked arrows pointing to which way the entrance is, in addition to the fact that since this is a drive up ATM it makes sense for the machine to be on the left side where the driver would be sitting. That said, it’s very easy for people to turn I to the outcropping the wrong way. This happened today while I went to get some cash. I arrived at my bank and as I took the turn to go into the ATM cut out, another car whipped into it going the wrong way so that their passenger could use the ATM. I was annoyed at this as I was just about to pull up to it and I was in kind of a hurry, since I needed to get to class. She took 15 minutes to do her transactions. She went through at least 3 cards inserting and reinserting the cards at least 2 times each. I sat patiently, yet annoyed, and waited for her to finish. But when she was done was reaching my limit of patience, she then leant out the window of her car and yell at me to move, I didn’t respond, no one was waiting behind me, I had already been late to class, so being more late wouldn’t kill me. I didn’t move. After about 5 minutes of her shouting at me to move, she backed up did a K-turn and left. I told my friend about this when I eventually arrived at class and he told me that I was being a dick for not just backing up since there was no one behind me. However I stick to the notion that I was in the right for not moving because they were going against traffic. AITA?

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. Driving wrong-way is illegal and dangerous (e.g., risk of head-on collisions if others enter from the opposite direction). - **Your right to the space**: Since you arrived first and were already in the correct lane, you had a **prior claim** to the ATM. Standing your ground sends a message that such behavior won’t be tolerated. 3. **Your Emotional State**: - You were **already late to class**, which added stress. While patience is ideal, your annoyance is human—especially when someone else’s actions directly inconvenience you *and* create a risky situation. 4. **Legal Precedent**: - In many jurisdictions, **blocking traffic** (even unintentionally) can be cited for violations like "obstructing traffic" or "failure to yield." Your stance aligns with the idea that wrong-way drivers should yield to correct traffic flow. --- ### **Why Your Friend’s Perspective Also Makes Sense (Score: ~0.6/1)** 1. **Etiquette and Practicality**: - **No one was behind you**: If no one else was waiting, your refusal to move could be seen as **petty or unnecessary**. The woman was already causing a delay (15 minutes of fumbling with cards), and your stand-off added to her frustration. - **ATMs are for quick access**: The ATM’s purpose is to serve *anyone* who needs it, not just those who arrive first. Wrong-way drivers might not realize they’re in the wrong until they’re already there, and forcing them to leave could deny them service entirely. 2. **Escalation Risk**: - **Her yelling was aggressive**, but your refusal to move could’ve escalated into a **road rage incident**. Your friend’s point is that sometimes, **de-escalation** (even if you’re "right") is the smarter choice to avoid conflict. - **Alternative solutions**: You could’ve politely asked her to back up (e.g., "Excuse me, you’re going the wrong way—could you turn around?") instead of silent defiance. 3. **Bank’s Responsibility**: - The bank’s ATM design might be **poorly marked**. If the arrows are unclear or the cutout is confusing, the fault could lie with the bank for not making it obvious. In that case, your refusal to move might seem like **holding a vulnerable driver accountable for a systemic issue**. 4. **Time vs. Principle**: - You were **already late**, and being more late wouldn’t "kill you." Your friend’s logic is that **principles matter less than consequences** in this case—your stand-off cost you nothing beyond a few extra minutes. --- ### **The Verdict: A Shade of Gray (Score: ~0.5/1)** This isn’t a clear-cut "AITA" scenario because: - **You weren’t wrong** for refusing to move *on principle* (wrong-way drivers should yield), but **you weren’t entirely right** because: - **Her actions were reckless**, but your **silent defiance** (without communication) made the situation worse. - **No one was behind you**, so your refusal to move wasn’t *actively* harming anyone—just being stubborn. - **Her yelling was unreasonable**, but your refusal to engage (even with a simple "Please back up") left no room for compromise. #### **Where You Could’ve Improved**: 1. **Communicate**: A simple **"Excuse me, you’re going the wrong way—could you turn around?"** would’ve been polite but firm. Your silence made it seem like you were *choosing* to hold her hostage. 2. **Assess the situation**: Since no one was behind you, your refusal to move wasn’t *necessary* for safety—just for principle. Principles are great, but **practicality matters too**. 3. **Consider the bank’s design**: If the ATM is poorly marked, the bank should fix it, not you. #### **Where She Was Wrong**: - **Wrong-way driving** is illegal and dangerous. She had no right to assume the space. - **Yelling at you** was uncalled for—she could’ve just backed up without escalating. - **Wasting time**: Her 15-minute fumbling with cards was already inconvenient; your refusal to move added to her stress. --- ### **Final Score: ~0.5/1 (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong)** - **You**: **0.7/1** for standing your ground on principle/safety, but **0.3/1** for not communicating or considering practicality. - **Her**: **0.3/1** for wrong-way driving and yelling, but **0.7/1** for being a first-time offender (maybe she didn’t realize she was wrong). **Best Outcome**: You could’ve said something like: *"Excuse me, you’re going the wrong way—could you back up? I was here first, but I’ll wait if you need to fix it."* This keeps it **polite, firm, and solution-oriented**. --- ### **Key Takeaway** Traffic etiquette is about **balance**: respecting rules *and* people. Your instinct to prioritize safety and order was good, but **how you handled it** could’ve been smoother. Next time, **communicate first, stand your ground second**.
